about: Photo look with real Hubble and Webb pictures: how stars are born, shine and die.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI; J. DePasquale, A. Koekemoer, A. Pagan (STScI) (CC BY 4.0)

scenes.narration: Stars are born in cold, dark clouds of gas and dust, like these pillars, each several light years tall.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, M. Livio and the Hubble 20th Anniversary Team (STScI) (CC BY 4.0)

scenes.narration: Gravity pulls the gas together until the centre reaches about ten million degrees. Then hydrogen fuses into helium, and a star switches on.
Our Sun turns about four million tonnes of itself into energy every second. It has done so for four and a half billion years.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA), A. Nota (ESA/STScI), and the Westerlund 2 Science Team The original observations of Westerlund 2 were obtained by the science team: Antonella Nota (ESA/STScI), Elena Sabbi (STScI), Eva Grebel and Peter Zeidler (Astronomisches Rechen-Institut Heidelberg), Monica Tosi (INAF, Osservatorio Astronomico di Bologna), Alceste Bonanos (National Observatory of Athens, Astronomical Institute), Carol Christian (STScI/AURA) and Selma de Mink (University of Amsterdam). Follow-up observations were made by the Hubble Heritage team: Zoltan Levay (STScI), Max Mutchler, Jennifer Mack, Lisa Frattare, Shelly Meyett, Mario Livio, Carol Christian (STScI/AURA), and Keith Noll (NASA/GSFC) (CC BY 4.0)

scenes.narration: Small, cool red stars can shine for trillions of years. The biggest, brightest stars burn out in just a few million.

image.credit: ESA/Webb, NASA, CSA, M. Barlow, N. Cox, R. Wesson (CC BY 4.0)

scenes.narration: A star like the Sun ends gently. It swells, then puffs its outer layers into space, leaving a glowing ring around a tiny white dwarf.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, T. Temim (Princeton University) (CC BY 4.0)

scenes.narration: A giant star ends in a supernova, bright enough to outshine its whole galaxy. This is the wreckage of one seen on Earth in the year ten fifty four.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, D. Milisavljevic (Purdue University), T. Temim (Princeton University), I. De Looze (University of Gent) (CC BY 4.0)

params.headline: A teaspoon weighs billions of tonnes.

scenes.narration: What is left behind can be a neutron star. A teaspoon of it would weigh billions of tonnes.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, and STScI (CC BY 4.0)

scenes.narration: The calcium in your bones and the oxygen you breathe were made inside stars that lived and died before the Sun was born.
